Private Members' Business
to any province that cuts down in terms of education, health care or social services for any child.
A similar experience happened in the United States when singing Jim Folson, the governor of Tennessee, decided that he was going to use welfare money for children for other purposes. The federal government in the United States had enough guts to cut off the money and force him to meet the standards. We can do the same thing with reluctant premiers here in this country. They are not reluctant because they are mean people, Mr. Speaker. They are reluctant because they are largely unaware of how serious the problem is for children in this country.
I want to comment about some of the changes that I have seen as I conclude my remarks. Some of the changes are in the use of alcohol and other drugs.
I hear pious words about a war on drugs. The most serious drug affecting children in our society and almost condoned by many parents is alcohol. There are some parents who actually believe that they are relieved that their kids are drinking beer or booze and not using drugs. Alcohol is a drug and it is a violently abused drug here in this country simply because in many instances it is pushed on kids through some of the advertising that is subtle but direct.
The last comment I want to make is about child sex abuse. The Badgley Report initiated by the Liberal government is a masterful example of the use of the House to bring information to legislators. The government is to be commended for releasing the Badgley Report, an outstanding piece of work showing unanimity about gathering facts. The Badgley Report, after gathering facts, is now gathering dust.
The statistics on increasing sexual abuse of children in this country are alarming and inexcusable and regrettably have reached into institutions where we never expected to encounter such behaviour. We have never as a nation made a commitment to ensure that a whole range of services are available for every child in this country regardless of race, creed or colour and that the services are available on the basis of the needs of the child rather than having the child fit into the services that the state thinks it needs. That means flexibility. It means some caution, some prudence and some understanding that at the bottom of all of this is money and a commitment.
I will be the first to go public and praise the Tory government if it accepts this motion, passes it and puts its money behind it. But if this is just to be another exercise for an afternoon, all of us being good and talking about the needs of children, then forget it. It will go down as another cynical and hypocritical afternoon. This is a rare chance in the legislative process to do something that means something for all of us and to back it up with money. I beg the government to take the chance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the Hon. Member for Mission-Coquitlam for placing this motion before the House because it gives us a chance to visit a subject sorely in need of greater attention. I rise to speak because I share her concern that we must do all that is possible to protect children and ensure their rights.
There are a lot of things that have happened in this century that would make us wonder whether civilization is advancing. But one of the marks of civilization perhaps is the extent to which we take care and consideration for the weaker, the more vulnerable, the voiceless, be they minorities, individuals with disabilities, the environment, animals, and most of all children. An effort to curb the strong is sometimes needed but efforts to uphold the weak is very much always there. A mark of how we can make progress on that is perhaps more than anything a mark of how civilized we are.
A comprehensive Canadian bill of rights for children is an admirable concept. But, in fact, there is a more immediate and practical alternative before us to accomplish the very same objective. I refer, as the hon. member herself did, to the United Nations Draft Convention on the Rights of the Child. This important international convention is expected to be adopted by the United Nations General Assembly later this year. Once adopted, the convention will be open to ratification by all countries, including Canada. States that become party to that international convention will be bound by the specific provisions, as the hon. member has pointed out, and the obligations that are contained in it.
September 25, 1989

How does that convention affect the debate within Canada? I think it is precisely that way. The hon. member herself referred to the high standards that are in that draft convention. I believe, to answer my own question, that this instrument developed through the comity of nations can serve as a bill of rights for children not only internationally but also domestically. We will go through the process to which she referred of seeing that all Canadian laws and policies reflect the new rights and obligations set out in that charter.
In the thirty-third Parliament I chaired a committee of this House on equality rights that went through essentially the same exercise dealing with Article 15 of the Charter. We looked at existing Canadian laws and programs to see that they in fact comply with the guarantees of equality enshrined in Article 15. A similar process is contemplated here.
I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who, unfortunately, put a negative cast on his remarks in referring to the government because the reality is that this country has taken a very active role in the development of this convention. He also gave a list of issues that affect the position of children in our society indicating which fall under federal and which fall under provincial jurisdiction. We are not hearing of that for the first time. Our government is more than mindful that these are mostly shared jurisdiction or provincial jurisdiction issues. That is why for some many months now the Government of Canada has worked closely with provincial governments to see that in the drafting of the convention itself their interests and concerns were adequately reflected. This is something that has been proceeding with care, pressing on toward this goal of having an instrument that can serve both the international community and, most assuredly, our own domestic situation with the best possible statement of the rights of children.
[Translation\
Mr. Speaker, we may ask here whether it is really necessary to have an international or national charter of children's rights. After all, children are human beings and as such should enjoy the rights provided in international instruments and national charters like our own Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Some states expto have an international or national charter of children's rights. After all, chilldren are human beings and as such should
Private Members' Business
enjoy the rights provided in international instruments and national charters like our own Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Some states expressed this opinion when the question of a convention on the rights of the child arose in the late 1970s.
Although we all agree that children enjoy the same basic rights as adults, we must still admit that they cannot exercise them all in the same way as adults and that furthermore, children require special protection much more than adults. The international community has recognized this fact since the beginning of the century. For example, The Hague Convention on the Laws of War adopted in 1907 is one of the first international instruments to deal with children's rights. This document and those that followed it set forth what protection must be given to children in wartime. The signatory states are required to provide this protection. The standards were considerably improved after the horrors of World War II, when the international community, meeting under the auspices of the Red Cross, wrote the four Geneva Conventions in 1949.

Outside of those specific areas of protection of children during armed conflict to which I have just referred, the international community took an early interest in the broader rights of the child. For example, in 1924, it was the League of Nations that adopted the first declaration of the rights of the child which, in these circles, is commonly referred to as the Declaration of Geneva. Although its content was only declaratory in nature, it did provide a necessary focus that has since guided the international community's work in this field of children's rights. It is worth noting that back in the mid-1920s a statement was made which says-and I think back to what the hon. member from British Columbia just said-that mankind owes to the child the best that it has to give-a simple, but a high standard. Sadly, in practice, that duty has often not been fulfilled.
It was because of those failings and the failings that other hon. members have documented here, Mr. Speaker, that the international community recognized it was necessary to ensure better protection for children. That is why in 1959 the UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child went some way toward achieving the goal of setting standards. Still, by the 1970s, as new issues affecting children came to the attention of all of us, it was recognized that a number of those provisions were

Adjournment Debate
simply out of date and that we had come to an era where a legally binding instrument was the order of the day.
It has been 10 years since then that this UN convention has been in the making. There have been countless difficulties and problems that probably would have derailed a less noble venture. There was the early problem of skepticism. Drafting this new convention was also plagued initially by cold war ideological disputes, not to mention the cultural differences of participating states which periodically resulted in quite a strong difference of opinion.
The working group in which Canada was very much an active participant persisted. This perseverance has resulted in a remarkable document that itself is testament, I believe, to the international community's continuing concern for the rights of the child. That is our closest, best hope to move forward because it already represents a strong response by Canada, both federally and provincially. If we get that convention ratified this year, and Canada becomes a signatory and we bring our domestic laws into line with it, I think that a great distance will have been covered to bring the aspirations expressed here this afternoon into a reality.

Mr. Speaker, as did the Hon. Members who just spoke, I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Mission-Coquitlam (Ms. Langan) for presenting this motion.

I will give it a try, Mr. Speaker, because if any vulnerable group in our society needs the Government's protection, it is our children.
This Government, through various departments including National Health and Welfare and the Solicitor General's department, continues and will continue to live up to its commitment to protect and provide for the welfare of Canadian children.
Our commitment is straightforward and simple, Mr. Speaker. Every Every child in Canada should have a chance to grow up and develop into a healthy individual.
This is a very stimulating and also a very complex responsibility.
The challenge becomes even greater when we consider the needs of those who may be handicapped or otherwise disadvantaged. Mr. Speaker, earlier we heard the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) explain the various programs provided by the Minister of National. In fact, I would have liked to expand on the measures proposed by the Solicitor General's department. Unfortunately, I do not have enough time.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-WAR AGAINST DRUGS.
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-WAR AGAINST DRUGS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say that today's question was postponed several times, although on several occasions I stayed in the House as late as ten o'clock at night, hoping to express my views on the very important subject of drug trafficking.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to thank you for this opportunity to pursue the subject raised in the House on May 31 in a question to the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Blais) about the war against drugs, further to the national annual report on drugs for 1987-88, published by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The report showed that enforcement techniques had improved and that international co-operation and the passage of new legislation on the profits of criminal behaviour will have a severe impact on major drug trafficking organizations. In the Western world, the RCMP has a solid reputation for its drug awareness programs.
Compared with 1986, the RCMP seized 41 per cent more cocaine and 94 per cent more cannabis in 1987. In Quebec, as part of its campaign against the profits of crime, it confiscated 25 per cent of those profits in the form of money and goods. These seizures concerned a total of $18.6 million, of which $4.8 million in Quebec. International trafficking in illegal drugs has increased spectacularly over the past few years, and apparently, drug profits are being used partly to finance terrorism.
The major organized groups that control the drug trade in Canada have established elaborate money laundering systems and are thus becoming increasingly powerful. In Canada, drug imports and sales generate between $5 and $10 billion annually. Montreal, where the number of users has tripled in the past two years, has confirmed its position as a focal point for the drug trade. Mr. Speaker, Montreal has between 10,000 and 15,000 of Canada's 25,000 heroin adddicts, while their number was estimated at only 5,000 at the beginning of 1987. Drug-related problems, including daily stress, personal and family problems, a higher incidence of criminal offences and traffic accidents as well as the rising cost of enforcement and health care, are a major social concern.
According to the Drug Addiction Research Foundation, the cost of drug abuse in Canada in 1984 totalled $11.5 billion. From 1976 to 1986, the number of viola-
Adjoumment Debate
tions of the Narcotics Act totalled 691,713. The number of persons convicted of these offences totalled 561,248.
The number of young people charged with a criminal offence under federal drug legislation was 4,767 in 1986 alone. More crimes, deaths, and disease will be inevitable in most Canadian cities if the expected increase in cocam and crack in the 90's materializes, since a report published by the mayor of Ottawa in June, Drug Abuse: Not my kid, revealed an increasingly serious problem with drug abuse.
Worse still, there is a shortage of treatment centres for youngsters under age 16. They must be sent to the United States, and that entails astronomical expenditures. Every day we can read newspaper articles on drugs and their devastating effects. Proliferating drug use creates a new threat to national security: the value of life is minimized, crime soars, and youg people ruin their lives for ever.
Police forces in the riding of Drummond have given priority to the fight against drugs. I am proud indeed to say that a commendable effort is being made in schools and within the whole community under the supervision of Director General Marcel Lefebvre and constable Remi Thibault.
Training programs have also been made available to the Drummond Penitentiary staff, and theirs is the most elaborate drug addiction program in Quebec.
In 1987 the Solicitor General of Canada announced the adoption of measures aimed at putting an end to drug trafficking. The Government has earmarked $210 million for this new strategy.
The Department of National Defence will provide more direct support in operations against drug dealers by making Canadian Forces aircraft and ships available to the RCMP.
The Minister of National Revenue announced that beginning last May 9 civil sanctions would be applied to discourage drug smuggling.
Other measures are to be taken to promote co-operation and an approach which reflects the national antidrug strategy.
Awareness and prevention programs alone however will not put an end to the availability of drugs and the dependence they create.

September 25, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, here is my question to the Solicitor General. Is it the Government's intention to introduce a stricter policy to fight against this insidious threat to our collective well-being by implementing strong measures to thwart drug dealers and users whose ranks have tripled over the past two years? All the more so because of the fact that, since President Bush unveiled his new antidrug program last September 5, drug dealers have been using Canada as a back door to gain access to the American market.
Considering that our media regularly report drug-related incidents, we have to come to the conclusion that we are before a fait accompli, an everyday occurrence.
In light of such deep concern, does the Government expect to increase border surveillance in an all-out antidrug war?

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-WAR AGAINST DRUGS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to compliment the Member for Drummond for his consistent and his persistent interest and concern about the plague that has hit Canada and western countries, indeed around the world, and that is the drug abuse that is going on that is killing, injuring and maiming children all around the world.
I think the member will recall that a few years ago our Prime Minister spoke in Vancouver about the epidemic proportion of the drug problem in Canada. He was criticized and lampooned by editorial boards across Canada for his alarmist statements regarding this problem. I think Canadians now realize that he was right and that the hon. member for Drummond is correct. I listened carefully to the remarks he made in his statement just now. He has done careful research on this subject. It is indeed a war that we are engaged in. The member has shown concerns in various levels about the welfare of children.
I have a letter from a very articulate mother regarding the plight of her 14-year old child whom she had cared for carefully. But she did not realize that in a matter of four months the child had moved from the use of marijuana, unknown to the parents, to the use of hard
drugs. Not even her best friends knew that the child was using this drug. This is the kind of a war that we are into.
The government is concerned that we attack it from every area we can. That is why the Department of Health and Welfare has initiated the national drug strategy and invested $210 million to educate young people and to attack this problem. That is why we have passed legislation, I think it is Bill C-61, whereby the government is now entitled to confiscate the profits from crime and in the first six months that that bill has been invoked, law enforcement officers have been able to confiscate $20 million across Canada from the profits of this crime.
That is just the beginning. I am sure that that is just the tip of the iceberg. The federal government is working with the provincial governments, through the RCMP, through the various agencies all across Canada, to educate, to apprehend and to confiscate. Those are the areas that we have to deal with and make sure that all levels of the government are co-operating in this war.
Again, I compliment the member for his intense pursuit of this subject because it is only if we in this House and people across the country take this same kind of intense interest in this subject that we will beat this war on drugs.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to expand on my question to the minister responsible for housing that I asked last April, and that was why he abandoned his position of principle and why he was no longer holding out the 30 per cent ratio of personal income as a realistic figure for housing. I think over the last number of years we have seen an increase in housing problems in this country, particularly in affordability.
I want to make it very clear when I express concern about the 30 per cent guideline that has been in place by CMHC as a maximum amount that a family should be spending on shelter, I am not in the least bit worried about the family that has an income of $6,000 a month and is spending $3,000 of it on a quarter of a million dollar home. My concern is for the woman who is looking after two children on an income of $1,000 a month and is
September 25, 1989

spending $600 a month or 60 per cent of her income, leaving the family with only $400 and living in poverty because on $400 she cannot buy the basic necessities of food, clothing and medical care.
We have seen in the last years a number of things happening in housing in this country. There has been a sharp increase in the price of housing, particularly in Toronto and Vancouver. However, the real estate board, last Thursday, at the finance committee said there are 22 markets, not just two in Vancouver, where a serious problem has arisen because of fast escalation of housing prices.
We have seen since 1980 a decline in real family income. Sixty per cent of all single parent families now are headed by women who live in poverty. One point two million children in this country are now living in poverty. The number of two parent families that live below the poverty line has doubled since 1973. What we are facing is a growing number of Canadians, not the wealthy but middle and lower income Canadians, who because of poverty cannot afford housing or because of the high cost of housing are being driven into poverty. They have always had at least the federal government saying you should not be paying more than 30 per cent. Some hope. And the minister has backed away from that.
This federal government has done a number of things that almost seem to be designed to take a bad problem and make it worse. Let me just list a couple of them. They have continued with their high interest rate policy. Every increase in the interest rate of 1 per cent adds $100 per month to the mortgage payment on a mortgage of $150,000. The other thing that they have done is they have backed away from social housing programs. They have reduced their commitment to provide non-market housing. We have seen that in the reduction in the number of units that they are willing to build under co-op housing and the doing away with the rental RRAP program. Rental RRAP was a significant program for the poor in some cities. It did not work universally well. We have an increased problem of poverty with renters in this country. Forty per cent of all renters now start with an income below the poverty line.
In my riding, in the last six months, as vacancy rates have gone down developers have taken over peripheral housing rental units, given them a coat of paint, put cheap carpets on the floor and have increased rents
Adjournment Debate
anywhere from 30 per cent to 50 per cent to 70 per cent, taking them totally out of the ability of people on fixed or marginal incomes to pay.
Now we have probably the most devastating blow on housing that anyone could take, and that is the GST. The government said it would give a rebate that would make housing not change in price. It estimated that there would be a net increase of only $480. Nobody believes that. The Home Builders Association has done its own independent calculations and it shows the price on a typical house costing $150,000 will increase $3,025, an increase over what the government said of 630 per cent.
I have had a tax firm, Oates Anderson, do some calculations for myself, considering not only the increase on the cost of housing, but the impact of inflation on the GST and the driving up of interest rates by GST. What Oates Anderson show is that it is not going to be the $480 that the federal government says, it is not even going to be the $3,000 that the Home Builders say, the increase could be as high as $14,000 on an average house in Vancouver, which means an increase in down payment of $3,600 and an increase in monthly mortgage payments of $230 on the average price in Vancouver.
So, I ask the minister again: What hope does he hold out? Instead of simply saying, "If the goal is not attainable, let us move the goalpost", I think he has to hold out some hope for Canadians for affordable housing, particularly those in the middle and lower income brackets .

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to make it quite clear that neither I nor the government have backed away from anything as far as helping Canadians with their housing problems.
I think the hon. member referred in his original question and has referred this evening to this 30 per cent figure. I would like to make it quite clear what that 30 per cent figure is all about.
There really are two aspects to the magic number of 30 per cent. First if a Canadian goes out to apply for a mortgage to a bank or a trust company, he or she will not get that mortgage unless his or her income is in excess of the total principal interest payments that that Canadian will make on the mortgage plus municipal taxes. That is one part of what the 30 per cent figure means.

September 25, 1989
Adjournment Debate
The second relates to the question of assisted housing. That means you are not eligible for assisted housing under the rules and regulations in place unless your income exceeds 30 per cent; unless you are paying greater than 30 per cent of your income for your housing needs. Those are the two aspects referred to and to which the Hon. Member has been referring as far as the number 30 per cent is concerned in relation to housing.
I was quoted in The Globe and Mail back on April 24, with respect to this as follows: First, that Canadians can no longer assume 30 per cent of their income will buy reasonable accommodation. Second, that 30 per cent of income for housing is no longer realistic for many Canadians. I do not really believe that the hon. member can quarrel with those two statements. In fact, that is the case. Today, many Canadians have to spend much more than 30 per cent of their income on affordable housing. We need to tiy to make sure we can house as many Canadians as we possibly can. There is no question of backing away from the 30 per cent figure whatsoever.
What the government did when it came to power in 1984 was to put in place a new policy, a policy whereby all government housing money was directed toward the neediest, those who were spending in excess of 30 per cent of their income on housing. In fact, that was not the policy of the previous government. In fact, it has meant that about 40 per cent more needy people get housing assistance from that government funding than got assistance under the previous government's policy.
That sort of policy and the money that is spent by the government at the present time on assisted housing means that some 600,000 units or homes across the country receive assistance with housing. It means that this year will add something like 45,000 more assisted housing units to the total inventory of housing across the country.
That is the sort of thing we need to do. Unfortunately, that is not enough, obviously, and we have to do other things as well. Some of the things that the hon. member is aware we are trying to do at the moment are, first, make some more surplus government land available for housing that is affordable to Canadians. Hopefully, we
will be doing it in the Vancouver area. We have done some in the Toronto area. Hopefully we will be able to do more.
Second, we have put in place some tripartite committees, federal, provincial and municipal. There is one in Vancouver. It met on September 12 and it is aimed at getting more land in place to produce more housing that is affordable to Canadians.
Third, we hope very shortly to have in place a regulatory reform process aimed at cutting the cost of housing through cutting the red tape involved in putting housing on the market and also in trying to improve the zoning regulations so that the housing being built will not be monster houses as are many of the homes in Vancouver, but starter ones affordable to Canadians.

speechtext:

CANADA POST CORPORATION-REMARKS OF CONSTITUENT-MINISTER'S POSITION/PUBLIC RELATIONS ACTIVITIES

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, June 21,1 rose in this chamber during Question Period to ask the minister responsible for Canada Post about newspaper advertising carrying the signatures of community leaders from across Canada, including one from my own constituency.
What prompted me to rise was that preceding that date, on June 15, the Minister had quoted from this advertisement in this House of Commons naming my constituent and identifying his community of residence. I later contacted my constituent to find out more concerning the Canada Post ads of which the minister was most proud. To be clear, the ads in question state: "People in my community are benefiting from this postal service. It is good for the community". That statement is followed by 80 signatures of reeves, mayors and councillors from across the country.
Before proceeding with the problems with the specifics of the ad itself, I would like to mention the context in which that ad occurred. That context is an odious one. The advertising campaign of which this ad is a part aims to convince rural Canadians that Canada Post is in rural Canada to stay. As rural Canadians with whom I am familiar know all too well this is not the case.
September 25, 1989

Canada Post and the federal government along with it is pulling out of rural Canada. Why, Mr. Speaker? Canada Post and this federal government are using rural Canadians as scapegoats in their single-minded pursuit of profits for Canada Post at the expense of service, at the expense of jobs for rural Canadians, and at the expense of the communities themselves.
My constituent named in this House of Commons, Mr. Edward Kjargaard, is listed from Alticane, Saskatchewan, where some changes in postal service have taken place. What used to be a thriving community with three grain elevators is now just a hamlet with maybe 15 people. Mr. Kjargaard is not the reeve of Alticane, he is the reeve of the RM of Douglas in which the hamlet of Alticane is situated. He lives 30 miles from Alticane and gets his mail not from outdoor boxes at Alticane but from a rural route delivery service which originates in the urban centre of North Battleford. Mr. Kjargaard made this all very clear to the Optima Research employee who visited him to discuss post office services in Alticane. To make a long story very short, my constituent said he had a good conversation with the person from Optima, but had he known it would turn out the way it did, he never would have signed the release they gave him to sign. In fact he admitted it seemed that Canada Post was more interested in his signature than in his opinion.
To substantiate his words, Mr. Kjargaard has sent me a letter in which he states:
Canada Post published my name in an advertising campaign but
they never mentioned my concerns.
While all this was going on media reporters and politicians have called others quoted in that advertising campaign. As many as 10 of those 80 people have said that their signatures were used in a manner different than what they expected.
I asked the minister to apologize to my constituents, and to all of Canada, for allowing Canada Post to cany an advertising campaign which misrepresents the truth. I asked the minister to explain how Canadians could be expected to trust him and Canada Post in the future if this is the way they conduct their public business.
The government has chosen to place the interests of big business and the Conservative quest for privatization at any cost before the day-to-day needs of all Canadians for an efficient, reliable, accountable postal service. This government has chosen to condone Canada Post's ill-conceived attempt to fool all of the people all of the time with its multi-million dollar advertising campaign and to
Adjournment Debate
condone Canada Post's misrepresentation of rural Canadians as they have done with this ad in question.
Therefore, I call on the government to listen to rural Canadians, to listen to the communities of Elbow, Lintlaw, Dubuc, Denzil and Wilkie, Saskatchewan as well as all the other rural communities across Canada including those in Prince Edward Island where this summer municipal leaders across the island said "no" to retail postal outlets.
I call on the government to listen to these Canadians, to put service and jobs before profits, to fulfil the mandate of Canada Post to provide service and, therefore, to put an end to costly ad campaigns which misrepresent Canadians and to insist that Canada Post get back to providing and expanding service to all. [Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I find it somewhat strange that the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Taylor) would seem fit to raise this question again, since it already was put in exactly the same terms and the Minister gave a very clear answer, both as to the procedure followed to canvars luminaries or municipal elected city officials as to whether they supported an advertising campaign, whether they were willing to have their names published during an advertisement campaign they were very clearly informed as to the nature of what that campaign, its theme and advertisement contents. They were asked in the questionnaire to sign a release for their names to be published.
Although unhappy if someone mistakenly signed such a simple statement, I can only repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the statement on which the ads were based reads: "People in my community are enjoying this new postal service, it is good for the community". They were asked to sign the following form: "I basically agree with the above statement and I hereby authorize Post Canada to use my name as a municipal representative who believes that people in my community are benefitting from the new postal service". That very simple form was indeed signed.
I would therefore ask the Hon. Member to understand. His question was duly answered. Now he raises the matter again. Now, his statement includes a number of unsubstantiated allegations. We had a scientifically-made survey, the data are available, it was done by Gallup-97 per cent of rural Canadians are satisfied with the Canadian postal service and the reform of the postal system. Let me now repeat what the Minister told him.

September 25, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Presumably he represents the other 3 per cent, which would explain his question, but our policy is based on the other 97 per cent of Canadians.
